Actually my assertion would be purely based upon usage in the world.
The two languages spoken by the greatest number of people have gender-
differentiated pronouns. Those languages would be Mandarin Chinese
and English.

a single word replaceing "I, Me".

Just as a side-note. The use of saying that something is "hot" to mean
it is "some degree of good" and using "cool" to do the same thing
comes from the Jazz movement in the 30s-60s. There was a group of
jazz musicians who tended to play fast, many-note type
improvisation... amongst themselves they called it "hot jazz" and also
tended to say such things as "that is hot" to indicate their approval
of the playing. A counter-movement began doing the opposite and
aiming for tone, harmony and slow-note playing. As a counter-movement
using the word "hot" was an insult and instead became the "cool jazz"
movement; where saying someone's playing was "cool" was to approve of
it. It SLOWLY seeped into a broader culture as jazz moved into
broader culture.

The same usage conventions that make "xe" a word at come into play for
"they" being used as a singular gender-neutral pronoun. With the
notable difference that one has a widely accepted usage which is clear
to the vast majority of speakers, and the other doesn't. Also, "you"

Pennsylvania there is a "yin" used for the plural second person, but

issue, but one isn't even found in the vast majority of dictionaries,
and is hard in a vacuum to find the definition for, so it seems even
that issue wouldn't support usage of "xe".

Alrighty, speaking from personal experience.

I failed my major in second year university. No sugar coating. No
"deferred success". No counsellor giving me a back rub and telling me
it was alright. Just a big fat F and the realisation that I'd wasted
my cash on uni fees that year. And it was the kick in the behind that
I needed. It made me take stock, ask myself what I was doing there,
whether I really wanted to be doing what I was doing. And after
answering those questions I came back next year and topped my class.

Sometimes, people need to taste failure in order to succeed. Sure it
tastes like sh*t. But it makes you not want to taste it again and try
harder. Cutting the sh*t with sugar and comforting words and hand
holding makes it easier to swallow, and the thought of swallowing it
again easier to take.

The school where my sister teaches gives all kids who compete in the
sports day a ribbon, out of some attempt, I suppose, to reward
participation. To my mind, all it does is reward mediocrity. Some kids
aren't good at sport, some aren't good at maths or art or english.
You don't get a prize in the real world for being average, for working
at Mickey D's or a 7-11. If you fail at your job, you generally get
fired (unless you're a public servant). This is life. Taking the sting
off failure makes it easier to accept, and more likely that you'll
accept it in future, rather that trying, desperately, to never taste
that horrible sh*t again.

jase

In English, words don't have "masculine" forms in the way that they
often do in other languages.

Often words adopted into English come from words that have a masculine
or feminine form ("sombrero", for example). But English tends to
ignore that sort of thing.

is currently a completely gender neutral term. Calling someone a

genderless term, why can't "he"? Well, 'cause "he" specifically refers

does not imply a gender one way or the other. Calling someone of
indeterminate gender "he" implies that he or she is a male, until more
information is gained.

-Peter
